title: A Name Cleared Poorly
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 30 of 40
content:
By evening, the newspapers had decided Snape had been exonerated.

He was furious.

“This is not what happened.”

He threw the Daily Prophet onto the table.

The headline read SNAPE CLEARED: SECRET HERO OF HOGWARTS.

I winced.

“Secret hero is going to bother you more than cleared, isn't it?”

“They are both inaccurate.”

“The hearing cleared you of prosecution.”

“It did not clear my life.”

“No.”

“And secret hero sounds like a children's serial.”

“That part is funny.”

“It is not.”

“It is a little.”

He glared.

We were back at Hogwarts, safely below ground, with the door locked against journalists and most of humanity.

McGonagall had ordered dinner sent down because Snape had refused the Great Hall.

There was soup.

There was bread.

There was an entire bottle of Ogden's Firewhisky that I suspected had come from her personal cabinet.

Snape examined it.

“Minerva has become reckless.”

“She's celebrating.”

“What?”

“You not going to prison.”

“An unnecessarily dramatic benchmark.”

“Low standards have served me well.”

His mouth twitched.

He poured two fingers into one glass.

Then looked at me.

“One?”

“Small.”

He poured half as much into mine.

We sat at the central table.

For several minutes neither of us spoke.

The hearing had exhausted language.

I sipped the whisky.

Snape stared at his.

“How do you feel?” I asked.

“Do you want the answer suitable for print?”

“No.”

“Annoyed.”

“That one is always suitable for print.”

“Relieved.”

The word came quietly.

I waited.

“And ashamed of being relieved.”

“Why?”

“Because there are dead people who received no hearing.”

The war entered the room again.

It always would.

“That doesn't mean you should have wanted punishment for its own sake.”

“No.”

“Do you believe the decision was fair?”

He considered.

“Legally? Yes.”

“Morally?”

“A government chamber is not equipped to answer that.”

“Good memory.”

He looked at me.

“You said it first.”

“I know. I'm delighted you listened.”

“I listen more often than you deserve.”

Warmth returned by degrees.

I broke bread.

Snape ate soup.

Eventually I said, “You asked me to wait until after.”

He went still.

“Yes.”

“It is after.”

“Yes.”

My pulse quickened.

He put down his spoon.

“I do not know what happens now.”

“Neither do I.”

“That does not concern you?”

“Of course it concerns me.”

“You appear calm.”

“I'm performing competence.”

His mouth curved.

“I recognize the technique.”

I laughed softly.

Snape looked at his hands.

“I have not done this.”

“What?”

His expression tightened.

“Had a relationship.”

The word sounded foreign in his mouth.

I knew enough about his life not to make assumptions about every private year, but the admission still startled me.

“Never?”

“Nothing I would call one.”

“Okay.”

“That is all?”

“What response were you expecting?”

“Concern.”

“I am concerned.”

His eyebrow rose.

“I am concerned you're going to treat dating like an advanced Potions examination.”

His face became offended.

“I would never.”

“You made rules for a shared laboratory on day three.”

“You suggested them.”

“You added amendments.”

“Because yours were poorly drafted.”

“See?”

He almost smiled.

I leaned forward.

“We can make rules if you need them.”

His eyes sharpened.

“Mocking me?”

“No.”

The humor faded.

“Boundaries help. So does clarity. We already know that.”

He looked at me for a long moment.

“Very well.”

I found a clean sheet of parchment.

Snape stared.

“You are serious.”

“Painfully.”

I wrote RELATIONSHIP RULES at the top.

He reached over, took the pen from my hand, and crossed out RULES.

He replaced it with AGREEMENTS.

I looked at him.

“That is better.”

“Yes.”

Agreement one: either person can say no without punishment.

Agreement two: asking for space must include, when possible, whether and when contact will resume. No disappearing as strategy.

Agreement three: anger is allowed. Deliberate cruelty is not.

Agreement four: no Legilimency without explicit permission.

Agreement five: no public disclosure of the relationship without mutual agreement.

Agreement six: neither person is required to compete with the dead.

I stopped writing.

Snape's hand went still beside mine.

“Too direct?” I asked.

“No.”

“You want it changed?”

“No.”

His voice was quiet.

I added it.

Agreement seven: no using gifts as debts.

Agreement eight: no pretending meals are optional during dangerous brewing.

Snape objected.

I refused.

Agreement nine: either person may revise the agreements by mutual consent.

Snape read the page.

“This is absurd.”

“Very.”

“It is also alarmingly sensible.”

“Thank you.”

“I did not compliment you.”

“You signed it.”

He had.

Severus Snape, in precise black fountain pen.

I signed beneath him.

Neither of us needed legal names spoken aloud for the story to know who I was.

He folded the parchment once.

“Where do we keep it?” I asked.

His gaze moved toward the hidden room.

Then back to me.

“My desk.”

Not hidden.

Not secret.

His desk.

I smiled.

“Careful.”

“Do not.”

“Trust.”

He rolled his eyes.

I stood and moved around the table.

Snape's attention sharpened.

“May I kiss you?” I asked.

His face softened.

“Yes.”

The kiss was warmer than the one in the storeroom.

Less frightened.

He touched my waist, paused for permission, then drew me closer when I leaned in.

I tasted whisky and soup and something that was simply him.

When we separated, his forehead rested against mine.

“Secret hero,” I whispered.

His eyes opened.

“I will end this relationship before it begins.”

I laughed.

“You signed an agreement.”

“It permits revision.”

“Mutual consent.”

His mouth curved.

“Damn.”

I kissed him again.

The newspaper remained on the table.

Snape's name had been cleared poorly.

We let the public get it wrong for one night.

Down in the dungeon, we knew what had actually happened.

He had been allowed to leave.

And this time, he chose where to go next.\n\nMuch later, after the castle had gone quiet and the Prophet had been folded face-down under a stack of inventory sheets, Snape made tea.\n\nThat alone told me the day had broken something loose. He usually treated tea as a beverage for people who lacked access to competent coffee.\n\nHe put too many leaves in the pot.\n\nI drank it anyway.\n\n“What happens now?” I asked.\n\nSnape stood by the worktable with his cup untouched. “An appalling number of forms.”\n\n“I meant after the forms.”\n\n“I am aware.”\n\nHe looked around the dungeon. The evidence seals were mostly gone now. Shelves had been repaired. Student cauldrons waited in orderly stacks for a school year that would begin whether anyone felt ready or not.\n\n“You could stay here,” I said.\n\n“I could.”\n\n“Do you want to?”\n\nHis gaze dropped to his tea. “I don't know.”\n\nThat answer no longer startled me. It had become one of the strangest signs of trust between us.\n\n“Spinner's End?” I asked.\n\nHis expression closed slightly.\n\n“The house remains.”\n\n“That's not the same as wanting to live there.”\n\n“No.”\n\n“Do you need to go back?”\n\nHe was silent long enough that I expected him to refuse the question.\n\n“Yes.”\n\nI nodded. “Then go back.”\n\nHis eyes narrowed. “That uncomplicated?”\n\n“No. But the first step can be.”\n\n“You have developed an unfortunate fondness for aphorisms.”\n\n“I spend too much time around old professors.”\n\n“I am thirty-eight.”\n\n“Ancient.”\n\n“Leave.”\n\n“You made tea.”\n\n“A regrettable lapse.”\n\nI smiled into my cup.\n\nHe watched me for a moment. “Will you come?”\n\nThe question was so quiet I nearly missed it.\n\n“To Spinner's End?”\n\n“Yes.”\n\n“If you want me to.”\n\n“I would not have asked otherwise.”\n\n“That has not historically been true of you.”\n\nHis eyes flashed.\n\nI held up one hand. “Sorry. Cheap shot.”\n\nSnape looked away. “Accurate, nonetheless.”\n\nI set down my cup. “Then yes. I'll come.”\n\nHe nodded once.\n\nThe plan formed in pieces after that. We would wait until the press found a newer corpse to resurrect. We would go in daylight. We would check the wards before entering. I would not touch anything in the upstairs bedroom without asking. He would not decide on my behalf that I was too uncomfortable to stay.\n\n“That last condition is absurd,” he said.\n\n“That last condition exists because you keep trying to protect people by removing their choices.”\n\n“I do not.”\n\nI looked at him.\n\nHe glared back.\n\n“Frequently,” he amended.\n\n“Thank you.”\n\n“There will be very little worth seeing.”\n\n“That's fine.”\n\n“The neighborhood is unpleasant.”\n\n“I've survived worse than a judgmental brick terrace.”\n\n“The neighbors are worse.”\n\n“I'll bring armor.”\n\nHe almost smiled.\n\nThe next morning a Ministry owl delivered the first packet confirming the terms of his release from formal review. Snape read every line twice. Then he placed the papers in a drawer instead of on the fire.\n\nThat mattered too.\n\nHis name had not been washed clean. He had not asked it to be.\n\nWhat he had been given was smaller and harder: permission to keep living with the truth intact.\n\nThree days later, we stood on a narrow pavement in Cokeworth beneath a sky the color of old pewter.\n\nAcross the street, Spinner's End leaned into the wind.\n\nSnape stared at the house.\n\n“So,” I said. “Still standing.”\n\nHe looked offended.\n\nWhich, somehow, made me less afraid of going inside.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
